power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Low-intensity focused ultrasound (LIFU) is a noninvasive neuromodulation technique that uses acoustic energy to modulate neural activity.
LIFU reaches both cortical and deep brain structures with millimeter precision, making it a candidate treatment approach for various neuropsychiatric conditions.

The neuromodulatory eMects of LIFU depend on the acoustic parameters of the protocol in conjunction with the underlying neurobiology of the target, though the mechanisms underlying these eMects are still being characterized.
Early clinical work spans depression, anxiety, substance use disorder, epilepsy, Parkinson's disease, and Alzheimer's disease, with trials that remain small and heterogeneous in target and protocol.

Here we review the state of the field, covering how LIFU is delivered, the mechanisms proposed to underlie its eMects, the evidence for target engagement in humans, and the clinical literature to date.
In addition to investigating LIFU's clinical eMicacy, considerable foundational work remains before LIFU can be eMectively deployed as a therapy.
Overall, LIFU has considerable potential, but rigorous mechanistic and clinical research will be essential to define its therapeutic role.
Low-intensity focused ultrasound (LIFU) is a noninvasive neuromodulation technique under active investigation as a therapeutic approach for a range of psychiatric and neurologic disorders.

Also known as transcranial ultrasound stimulation (TUS) or transcranial focused ultrasound stimulation (FUS; tFUS), LIFU is a noninvasive neuromodulation technique that combines a strong safety profile with the ability to precisely target deep brain structures [1] [2] [3] .
text.formatted: Also known as transcranial ultrasound stimulation (TUS) or transcranial focused ultrasound stimulation (FUS; tFUS), LIFU is a noninvasive neuromodulation technique that combines a strong safety profile with the ability to precisely target deep brain structures <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref> .

text.text: Early results across a range of conditions are promising, but much remains to be learned and refined, from elucidating its therapeutic mechanism(s) of action to establishing clinically eMective parameters and dosing.
Low-intensity focused ultrasound for neuromodulation is distinct from several other ultrasound-based neural therapeutics (Figure 1).
text.formatted: Low-intensity focused ultrasound for neuromodulation is distinct from several other ultrasound-based neural therapeutics (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">1</ref>).

text.text: Focused ultrasound, shaped narrowly toward a specific target, is distinct from unfocused ultrasound, which spreads acoustic energy across large brain regions, and is commonly used in diagnostic imaging 4 .
text.formatted: Focused ultrasound, shaped narrowly toward a specific target, is distinct from unfocused ultrasound, which spreads acoustic energy across large brain regions, and is commonly used in diagnostic imaging <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref> .

text.text: Highintensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) delivers suMicient intensity at the focus to cause heatbased lesioning and is used clinically to noninvasively ablate parts of the thalamus and pallidum in essential tremor and Parkinson's disease.
LIFU delivers intensities orders of magnitude lower and does not cause lasting tissue damage 5 .
text.formatted: LIFU delivers intensities orders of magnitude lower and does not cause lasting tissue damage <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5</ref> .

text.text: Focused ultrasound at intermediate intensities can be used to temporarily open the blood-brain barrier for liquid biopsy 6 or targeted drug delivery: gas-filled microbubbles are injected into the bloodstream, and sonication drives them to oscillate in size, transiently disrupting the blood-brain barrier so that drugs can reach the brain 7 .

text.text: Like HIFU, this application generally requires intensities higher than the low-intensity focused ultrasound regime 8 (though not always see 9 ).

text.text: Because these biological eMects depend on the ultrasound intensity, a protocol intended to be low-intensity can enter damaging regimes if its parameters are not controlled [10] [11] [12] (Figure 1).

text.text: Clinical interest in LIFU for neuropsychiatric conditions has surged in recent years, with 150 new trials registered in the past five years alone 13 .
text.formatted: Clinical interest in LIFU for neuropsychiatric conditions has surged in recent years, with 150 new trials registered in the past five years alone <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13</ref> .

text.text: This interest builds on a broader expansion of interest in neuromodulation 14 .
text.formatted: This interest builds on a broader expansion of interest in neuromodulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14</ref> .

text.text: The most widely deployed neuromodulation tool available to patients is deep brain stimulation (DBS), which delivers electrical stimulation to a targeted brain region through implanted electrodes.
DBS is invasive, requiring surgical implantation, and any subsequent repositioning of the electrode requires additional surgery.

These drawbacks drive interest in scalable, noninvasive tools for targeted neuromodulation, such as transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) and transcranial electrical stimulation (tES), which are FDA-approved treatments for some neuropsychiatric disorders like depression and OCD [14] [15] [16] .
text.formatted: These drawbacks drive interest in scalable, noninvasive tools for targeted neuromodulation, such as transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) and transcranial electrical stimulation (tES), which are FDA-approved treatments for some neuropsychiatric disorders like depression and OCD <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref> .

text.text: However, these modalities' direct eMects are confined to the cortical surface and can only modulate deep brain structures indirectly 14 .
text.formatted: However, these modalities' direct eMects are confined to the cortical surface and can only modulate deep brain structures indirectly <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14</ref> .

text.text: LIFU is positioned to address these limitations, reaching both cortical and subcortical structures with millimeter precision.
LIFU operates using high-frequency sound waves (typically in the 200-700 kHz range) to deliver mechanical pressure to brain structures along the sound path.

The pioneering ultrasound studies were conducted by Fry and colleagues in the 1950s, demonstrating the feasibility of using ultrasound to both modulate (low-intensity) and ablate (high-intensity) human neural tissue 17 (though also see the preclinical work by Harvey in 1929 18 ).
text.formatted: The pioneering ultrasound studies were conducted by Fry and colleagues in the 1950s, demonstrating the feasibility of using ultrasound to both modulate (low-intensity) and ablate (high-intensity) human neural tissue <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17</ref> (though also see the preclinical work by Harvey in 1929 <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18</ref> ).

text.text: However, these early studies required removing a section of the skull to avoid both surface tissue damage and distortions of the ultrasound beam caused by the skull, which impeded their practicality 19 .
text.formatted: However, these early studies required removing a section of the skull to avoid both surface tissue damage and distortions of the ultrasound beam caused by the skull, which impeded their practicality <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19</ref> .

text.text: Interest in ultrasonic neuromodulation resurfaced in the late 2000s, when Tyler and colleagues demonstrated in ex-vivo preparations then in rodent models that lowintensity ultrasound could evoke neuronal activity, a line of work that extended to the first transcranial human studies by 2014 [20] [21] [22] .

text.text: As computational modeling and neuroimaging have advanced in recent years, researchers can now simulate how the acoustic beam propagates and attenuates through intact, heterogeneous cranial bone to reach a specific target, enabling precise delivery of ultrasound to the brain without surgical intervention 19 .

text.text: This review covers the state of the field for low-intensity focused ultrasound: current best practices for its use, leading hypotheses concerning its mechanisms of action, and the evidence for its clinical utility across a range of neurologic and psychiatric conditions.
We also point the reader to additional reviews targeting specific subtopics in the field in Table 1.
text.formatted: We also point the reader to additional reviews targeting specific subtopics in the field in Table <ref type="table">1</ref>.

text.text: Focused ultrasound modulates neural activity by delivering ultrasonic pulses from an external transducer to an intracranial target.
The transducer converts electrical energy into mechanical energy through piezoelectric crystals mounted on its face.
An oscillating voltage makes these crystals expand and contract in thickness, generating pressure waves that radiate outward.
These waves are then focused with an acoustic lens.
A given LIFU protocol is defined by the properties of these waves: the fundamental frequency, the pulse regime, the intensity, and the duration (Figure 2).
text.formatted: A given LIFU protocol is defined by the properties of these waves: the fundamental frequency, the pulse regime, the intensity, and the duration (Figure <ref type="figure">2</ref>).

text.text: The fundamental frequency is the number of wave oscillations per unit time.
Higher fundamental frequencies produce tighter focal spots but attenuate more as they cross the skull 4 .
text.formatted: Higher fundamental frequencies produce tighter focal spots but attenuate more as they cross the skull <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref> .

text.text: The pulse regime comprises the pulse repetition frequency, the pulse duration, and the duty cycle; diMerent combinations of these parameters are thought to determine the magnitude and direction of the eMect, together with the underlying biology of the target 3, 4, 8, 23 .
text.formatted: The pulse regime comprises the pulse repetition frequency, the pulse duration, and the duty cycle; diMerent combinations of these parameters are thought to determine the magnitude and direction of the eMect, together with the underlying biology of the target <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23</ref> .

text.text: Ultrasound dose is characterized by two intensity measures that separately emphasize the mechanical and thermal eMects of the acoustic wave (Figure 2).
text.formatted: Ultrasound dose is characterized by two intensity measures that separately emphasize the mechanical and thermal eMects of the acoustic wave (Figure <ref type="figure">2</ref>).

text.text: The spatial-peak pulse average (ISPPA) is the average intensity over a single pulse and indexes the mechanical stress delivered during that pulse.
The spatial-peak temporal average (ISPTA) is the intensity averaged across the sonication duration, including the time between pulses, and indexes cumulative heating.

The corresponding safety limits (see below) follow this division: the mechanical index (MI), calculated from peak rarefactional pressure and fundamental frequency, approximates the likelihood of cavitation, while maximum thermal rise bounds tissue heating 4.
text.formatted: The corresponding safety limits (see below) follow this division: the mechanical index (MI), calculated from peak rarefactional pressure and fundamental frequency, approximates the likelihood of cavitation, while maximum thermal rise bounds tissue heating <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref>.

text.text: Because the skull attenuates, reflects, and distorts the acoustic beam, the intensity delivered to the target cannot be measured directly and is instead estimated by simulation 4 .
text.formatted: Because the skull attenuates, reflects, and distorts the acoustic beam, the intensity delivered to the target cannot be measured directly and is instead estimated by simulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref> .

text.text: These simulations use the patient's own CT and MRI images to model how bone thickness and density bend and weaken the beam, so that the protocol can be adjusted to deliver the intended dose.
While individual simulations are critical, establishing ground truth for dosing remains a challenge 24 .
text.formatted: While individual simulations are critical, establishing ground truth for dosing remains a challenge <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">24</ref> .

text.text: Transducers with many independently driven elements (phased arrays) can partly correct for this distortion by adjusting the timing across elements to reshape the beam through the skull and steer the focal target of the beam.

Additionally, there are transducers that use a single element or a small number of elements, in which case skull-induced distortion is accounted for during target planning rather than corrected in real time 4 .
text.formatted: Additionally, there are transducers that use a single element or a small number of elements, in which case skull-induced distortion is accounted for during target planning rather than corrected in real time <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref> .

text.text: Targeting is aided by neuronavigational approaches 4.
text.formatted: Targeting is aided by neuronavigational approaches <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref>.

text.text: The neuromodulatory eMects of LIFU are thought to arise from a complex interplay among the sonication parameters, the target's neurobiology, and the current physiological state.

The proximate physical cause is acoustic radiation force (the transfer of momentum from the pressure wave to the tissue it passes through), which strains elastic tissue and deforms the structures within it 4 .
text.formatted: The proximate physical cause is acoustic radiation force (the transfer of momentum from the pressure wave to the tissue it passes through), which strains elastic tissue and deforms the structures within it <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref> .

text.text: This force produces strain in proportion to the tissue's elasticity, which means the stiMness of the tissue determines how much mechanical deformation a given pressure delivers 23 .
text.formatted: This force produces strain in proportion to the tissue's elasticity, which means the stiMness of the tissue determines how much mechanical deformation a given pressure delivers <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23</ref> .

text.text: As the field has progressed, an increasing number of cell types, subcellular constituents, channels, and even components of the membrane glycoproteins and extracellular matrix have been shown to be mechanosensitive, and the response at any given target depends on which of these are present at the beam's focus (Figure 3).
text.formatted: As the field has progressed, an increasing number of cell types, subcellular constituents, channels, and even components of the membrane glycoproteins and extracellular matrix have been shown to be mechanosensitive, and the response at any given target depends on which of these are present at the beam's focus (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">3</ref>).

text.text: DiMerent mechanisms may also dominate at diMerent times: an important distinction is whether an eMect is 'online' , present during active sonication, or 'oMline' , persisting after the sonication terminates.

A parallel line of research asks whether a given protocol is inhibitory or excitatory of the overall neuronal activity within a brain region 29 , and here identical protocols can produce divergent eMects depending on the neurobiology of the target 22, 30 , including its balance of excitatory and inhibitory neurons, its complement of astrocytes, and its prevalence of Piezo and transient receptor potential (TRP) channels (Figure 3) 8, 23, 31 .
text.formatted: A parallel line of research asks whether a given protocol is inhibitory or excitatory of the overall neuronal activity within a brain region <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">29</ref> , and here identical protocols can produce divergent eMects depending on the neurobiology of the target <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">30</ref> , including its balance of excitatory and inhibitory neurons, its complement of astrocytes, and its prevalence of Piezo and transient receptor potential (TRP) channels (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">3</ref>) <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">31</ref> .

text.text: Mapping the ultrasound parameter space in conjunction with specific targets remains an important project for the field.
The most widely accepted mechanism of LIFU neuromodulation is that acoustic radiation force opens mechanosensitive ion channels 3, 8, 23 .
text.formatted: The most widely accepted mechanism of LIFU neuromodulation is that acoustic radiation force opens mechanosensitive ion channels <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23</ref> .

text.text: The best-characterized of these are non-selective cation channels that conduct calcium, sodium, and potassium upon membrane deformation by ultrasound vibrations, causing conformational changes and activation of the channels.

As calcium itself is a secondary messenger, the ultrasound-evoked calcium influx, in addition to depolarizing the membrane potential, triggers secondary intracellular signaling, such as recruiting other ion channels and activating intracellular enzymes and signaling cascades 32 .
text.formatted: As calcium itself is a secondary messenger, the ultrasound-evoked calcium influx, in addition to depolarizing the membrane potential, triggers secondary intracellular signaling, such as recruiting other ion channels and activating intracellular enzymes and signaling cascades <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">32</ref> .

text.text: TRPM4 has been implicated as one such amplifier, depolarizing the membrane in response to rising intracellular calcium 23, 32 .
text.formatted: TRPM4 has been implicated as one such amplifier, depolarizing the membrane in response to rising intracellular calcium <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">32</ref> .

text.text: Supporting this account, replacing the bath with calcium-free artificial cerebrospinal fluid abolishes the LIFU-induced depolarization 32 .
text.formatted: Supporting this account, replacing the bath with calcium-free artificial cerebrospinal fluid abolishes the LIFU-induced depolarization <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">32</ref> .

text.text: Beyond this acute depolarization, the same calcium entry triggers intracellular signaling cascades that can lead to transcriptional activation in the nucleus, including the upregulation of genes such as c-Fos and brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), which could mediate reported oMline eMects of sonication 8, 23.
text.formatted: Beyond this acute depolarization, the same calcium entry triggers intracellular signaling cascades that can lead to transcriptional activation in the nucleus, including the upregulation of genes such as c-Fos and brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), which could mediate reported oMline eMects of sonication <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23</ref>.

text.text: Many mechanosensitive ion channels have been implicated in the LIFU response, including Piezo1/2 channels, TRP channels, TREK and TRAAK channels, and NMDA receptors (Figure 3).
text.formatted: Many mechanosensitive ion channels have been implicated in the LIFU response, including Piezo1/2 channels, TRP channels, TREK and TRAAK channels, and NMDA receptors (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">3</ref>).

text.text: Piezo1 has been the most extensively studied: conditional knockout in mouse motor cortex reduces ultrasound-evoked calcium signaling, c-Fos expression, and behavioral readouts 33 , while Piezo1 expression in ultrasound-insensitive HEK cells confers ultrasound sensitivity 34 .
text.formatted: Piezo1 has been the most extensively studied: conditional knockout in mouse motor cortex reduces ultrasound-evoked calcium signaling, c-Fos expression, and behavioral readouts <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">33</ref> , while Piezo1 expression in ultrasound-insensitive HEK cells confers ultrasound sensitivity <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">34</ref> .

text.text: Piezo1 is expressed widely across cortical and subcortical regions, in the central and peripheral nervous systems, in neurons and glia, and in the vascular endothelium 3, 8, 25 .
text.formatted: Piezo1 is expressed widely across cortical and subcortical regions, in the central and peripheral nervous systems, in neurons and glia, and in the vascular endothelium <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25</ref> .

text.text: More recent work, however, suggests Piezo1 may be only moderately responsive relative to other candidates, with TRPC1 and TRPP2 showing stronger responses and TRPC6 reported as essential for ultrasound-induced excitability 32 .
text.formatted: More recent work, however, suggests Piezo1 may be only moderately responsive relative to other candidates, with TRPC1 and TRPP2 showing stronger responses and TRPC6 reported as essential for ultrasound-induced excitability <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">32</ref> .

text.text: Ultrasound may also modulate potassium flux by activating TREK1 and TRAAK channels 35, 36 , which are enriched at the nodes of Ranvier 37 .
text.formatted: Ultrasound may also modulate potassium flux by activating TREK1 and TRAAK channels <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">35,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">36</ref> , which are enriched at the nodes of Ranvier <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">37</ref> .

text.text: Because TRAAK conducts potassium outward, their opening hyperpolarizes the membrane and suppresses firing, raising the possibility that ultrasound may also modulate conduction in white matter tracts.
Finally, NMDA receptors have been shown to be moderately responsive to ultrasound 23, 32.
text.formatted: Finally, NMDA receptors have been shown to be moderately responsive to ultrasound <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">32</ref>.

text.text: The distribution of mechanosensitive channels across cell types, therefore, shapes how a given region responds to sonication.
A single protocol can produce short bursts of activity in mouse primary motor cortex but longer, rhythmic firing in the hippocampus 38 .
text.formatted: A single protocol can produce short bursts of activity in mouse primary motor cortex but longer, rhythmic firing in the hippocampus <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">38</ref> .

text.text: Cell-type composition oMers one account of such diMerences.

The neuronal intramembrane cavitation excitation (NICE) model predicts that particular protocols preferentially engage excitatory or inhibitory neurons, so that the net eMect at a target would depend on its ratio of the two 39 .
text.formatted: The neuronal intramembrane cavitation excitation (NICE) model predicts that particular protocols preferentially engage excitatory or inhibitory neurons, so that the net eMect at a target would depend on its ratio of the two <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">39</ref> .

text.text: This ratio varies substantially across the brain: roughly 80% of cortical neurons are excitatory, 70% of hippocampal neurons are excitatory, while 95% of striatal neurons are inhibitory 25, 40, 41 .
text.formatted: This ratio varies substantially across the brain: roughly 80% of cortical neurons are excitatory, 70% of hippocampal neurons are excitatory, while 95% of striatal neurons are inhibitory <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">40,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">41</ref> .

text.text: Empirical work supports the premise, with one parameter set increasing the activity of parvalbumin-expressing interneurons while suppressing excitatory neurons within the hippocampus 30 .
text.formatted: Empirical work supports the premise, with one parameter set increasing the activity of parvalbumin-expressing interneurons while suppressing excitatory neurons within the hippocampus <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">30</ref> .

text.text: Additionally, the same cells have been shown to respond diMerently to varying sonication parameters.
In one example using anesthetized rodents, increasing the PRF corresponded to increases in firing rates in excitatory, but not inhibitory, neurons 42 .
text.formatted: In one example using anesthetized rodents, increasing the PRF corresponded to increases in firing rates in excitatory, but not inhibitory, neurons <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">42</ref> .

text.text: Other reports have found that the response is even varied within cell types, where neurons of the same subclass at a single target can react diMerently to the same sonication 3 .
text.formatted: Other reports have found that the response is even varied within cell types, where neurons of the same subclass at a single target can react diMerently to the same sonication <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3</ref> .

text.text: Together, these findings indicate that a single protocol can produce varying eMects in diMerent regions, and that predicting the direction of an eMect may require knowing the cellular and channel composition of the sonication target.
Downstream and non-neuronal mechanisms: The brain's mechanosensitivity extends beyond the acute channel-level eMects described above.
Some of the durable, 'oMline' eMects could also arise from a broader set of responses, including those originating outside the neuron 3, 8, 23 .
text.formatted: Some of the durable, 'oMline' eMects could also arise from a broader set of responses, including those originating outside the neuron <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23</ref> .

text.text: This section covers five that have received the most attention: astrocytic signaling, microglial and inflammatory responses, vascular eMects, remodeling of the extracellular matrix, and the synaptic plasticity on which several of these converge (Figure 3).

text.text: Reviews covering additional proposed mechanisms, including flexoelectric eMects, sonoporation, microtubule resonance, lipid rafts, and a possible thermal contribution, are highlighted in Table 1, but are beyond the scope of this review.

text.text: As noted above, mechanosensitive channels are not confined to neurons.

Both Piezo1 and TRP channels are strongly expressed in astrocytes, where they mediate mechanically evoked calcium responses and glutamate release that, in turn, drives firing in neighboring neurons 2, 25, [43] [44] [45] .

text.text: The best-characterized route runs through TRPA1: ultrasound-evoked TRPA1 activation drives astrocytic glutamate release via Best1 channels, which activates synaptic NMDA receptors on neighboring neurons and produces a motor response in mice 23, 45 .

text.text: This account diMers from the cell-autonomous neuronal mechanism described above in assigning astrocytes and NMDA receptors a central role, and research to reconcile these accounts is ongoing 25, 32, 45 .

text.text: Other groups have found that astrocyte-specific Piezo1 knockout mice show impaired hippocampal long-term potentiation (LTP) and corresponding oMline deficits in learning and memory behaviors 44 .

text.text: Sonication additionally acts on the structures surrounding neurons and glia.

Emerging work shows that ultrasound alters neurovascular activity: in rodents, focused ultrasound induces microvascular vasodilation that persists for minutes after sonication ends 64, 65 , and in humans, an initial study found that ultrasound applied to the brachial artery produced arterial dilation lasting from 2 to 20 minutes post-sonication 66 .

text.text: Ultrasound also acts on the extracellular matrix, the macromolecular network that fills the space between cells and forms perineuronal nets around many neuronal cell bodies and dendrites 63, 67 .

text.text: Several of the mechanisms above converge on synaptic plasticity: calcium-driven c-FOS and BDNF expression, astrocytic neurotrophin release, and remodeling of the extracellular matrix all favor synaptic change, and each operates on a timescale longer than the sonication itself.

text.text: In summary, there is likely no single mechanism that drives the neuromodulatory changes after LIFU sonication.
While opening mechanosensitive ion channels is suMicient to modulate neuronal firing, a cascade of additional responses may contribute to or drive the therapeutic eMects.

Furthermore, the neurobiology of a given target, in conjunction with the sonication parameter set, likely determines whether the immediate or lasting eMects of sonication are excitatory or inhibitory, and this complexity may partially explain the heterogeneity in responses.

Basic research using LIFU in humans has focused on establishing target engagement via neuroimaging, electrophysiology, and behavioral readouts, exploring how target engagement changes under diMerent protocol parameters, and establishing best practices for handling confounds.

Target engagement-physiological readouts: Common methods for assessing target engagement leverage TMS-driven motor-evoked potentials (MEPs), sensory evoked potentials (SEPs), functional MRI, and novel MR sequences such as acoustic radiation force imaging (MR-ARFI).

When using MEPs, focused ultrasound is applied to a target such as the sensory thalamus or M1 while concurrent TMS pulses drive suprathreshold motor firing; the resulting MEP amplitude is then compared against sham or alternative ultrasound protocols.
SEP studies compare tactile, auditory, or visual evoked potentials before, during, or after sonication of sensory or thalamic regions to test for amplification or suppression of the evoked response.
Both task-based and resting-state fMRI have been used to probe local and connectivity changes around sonication.

Many fMRI studies have reported long-lasting oMline eMects 73, 74, 74, 75 , which have often been interpreted as evidence of LTP-or LTD-like plasticity, but ultrasound's eMects on the vasculature oMer an alternative or additional contribution, since the BOLD and perfusion signals that index connectivity are themselves vascular.

text.text: Disentangling the two is an active area of work, though the interpretations are not mutually exclusive: plasticity changes and vascular eMects could coexist, and methods such as arterial spin labeling are increasingly used to characterize the vascular component directly.
These diMiculties have also motivated MR sequences that specifically measure tissue displacement.

MR-ARFI localizes the acoustic focus by imaging the displacement produced by radiation force, confirming where energy was delivered rather than whether tissue responded, and work is ongoing to translate it to humans 76, 77.

text.text: Target engagement-behavioral readouts: LIFU applied to humans and nonhuman primates produces behavioral changes across a wide range of targets and tasks, spanning multiple cortical and subcortical areas 3, 78 .

text.text: As suggested by the proposed mechanisms of action, whether the reported eMects are facilitatory or inhibitory appears to depend on both the target and the protocol.

Across multiple subregions in the prefrontal cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, insula, and sensory cortices, sonication has produced facilitatory eMects on learning rate, choice, control, and discrimination tasks under some protocols 21, [79] [80] [81] [82] [83] [84] [85] [86] [87] and inhibitory eMects under others 74, 75, [88] [89] [90] [91] [92] [93] .

text.text: Furthermore, while facilitatory and inhibitory behavioral eMects have been reported across diMerent targets and protocols, how these behavioral changes emerge from shifts in neuronal suppression or excitation is often unclear.
The eMect sizes and durations of these changes also remain under investigation.
Parameter space: Predicting how changes to the protocol will translate into physiological or behavioral eMects remains poorly understood.
Some studies have directly compared the eMect of sonication when changing pulse repetition frequency (PRF), duty cycle, pulse duration, or intensity 29,100-103 .

For example, several studies showed that applying lower PRFs, such as 5 or 10 Hz resulted in neuromodulation that outlasted the sonication, with eMects enduring for 30 to 60 minutes 73, 74, 90, 100, 104 .

text.text: Few studies have compared long and short PRFs using the same design, however, and at least one of them found enduring eMects at higher PRFs as well 102 .

text.text: In terms of PRF's eMect on direction of eMect (e.g., inhibitory vs. excitatory), the pattern is even less settled.
At M1, much of the oMline work using lower PRFs reports excitatory eMects, using TMS-evoked MEP as the readout 100,105-107 .
However, across non-motor cortical targets, there have been reports of higher PRFs resulting in excitation 82 and lower PRFs resulting in inhibition 108 , with no studies directly comparing them.

text.text: Adding to these diMiculties, recent work has shown that eMects in many target-engagement studies may be driven in part by an auditory confound 103 .

text.text: Sonication produces an audible sound related to the PRF.

For example, in the standard MEP setup, the ultrasound pulse slightly precedes the TMS pulse, so participants can learn to anticipate the TMS pulse from the click; that anticipation alone alters the motor response.
The confound is not limited to human work.

Ultrasound activates the auditory system through a cochlear pathway in rodents, and deafening the animals or transecting the cochlear nerve abolishes much of the cortical response previously attributed to direct neuromodulation 109, 110 .

text.text: Clinical applications of low-intensity focused ultrasound remain in their infancy.
Most trials to date are small, single-arm studies of safety and feasibility, and the randomized controlled trials that exist are modest in size and heterogeneous in target, protocol, and indication.
The evidence is correspondingly preliminary.
Still, early signals across several conditions are encouraging enough to motivate the larger and better-controlled trials the field now needs.
The preliminary research in Parkinson's disease has concentrated on two targets: the globus pallidus internus (GPi) and the primary motor cortex (M1).
Lin et al. (2026) 111 compared bilateral M1, GPi, and simultaneous M1 and GPi theta-burst sonication in 13 patients on medication, using a randomized, blinded design.

text.text: Research on low-intensity focused ultrasound remains in its early days.

Foundational work is needed on several fronts, including standardizing how protocols are reported, establishing ground-truth estimates of the dose delivered to the target, and developing readouts that confirm target engagement.
Progress in these areas will allow the field to distinguish a protocol that failed to engage its target from one that engaged it but provided no therapeutic benefit.

Mechanistic work faces a parallel problem, since the direction and duration of an eMect depend on the target and the full parameter set in ways that are not currently predictable, and the systematic comparisons that would resolve this have largely not been done.
Most importantly, clinical eMicacy has yet to be established for any condition, target, or protocol.
However, these are tractable problems, and the field has already begun to address them.

By doing so, LIFU can expand the treatment landscape for the many neuropsychiatric patients who are still awaiting eMective solutions. causing a strain on the blood-brain barrier within the acoustic field; this intervention is currently being explored for opening the blood-brain barrier for drug delivery into the central nervous system and for conducting liquid biopsies.

text.text: A LIFU protocol is described at three nested timescales.
At the coarsest level (top), sonication is delivered as a series of pulse trains, characterized by the pulse train duration and the interval between successive trains.

Within a train (center), ultrasound is delivered as discrete pulses: the pulse duration (PD) is the time the transducer is emitting, the pulse repetition interval (PRI) is the time from the onset of one pulse to the onset of the next, and the pulse repetition frequency (PRF) is its reciprocal.
Duty cycle expresses the proportion of each interval during which ultrasound is being delivered.
Within a single pulse, the waveform oscillates at the fundamental frequency.

The two intensity metrics (bottom) differ in their averaging window: the spatial-peak pulse average (ISPPA) is the intensity averaged over the duration of a pulse, and is a function of peak pressure (p) and the acoustic impedance of the medium (Z), while the spatial-peak temporal average (ISPTA) is averaged across the full sonication and scales with duty cycle.

Figure 3.
Cellular and molecular mechanisms of LIFU neuromodulation.
(A) Tissue context.
Acoustic radiation force acts on all constituents within the ultrasound beam.
Excitatory and inhibitory neurons, astrocytes, and microglia, express mechanosensitive channels, so the response at a given target depends on which cell types are present and in what proportion.
Ultrasound also acts on the extracellular matrix, including the surrounding blood vessels.
(B) Neuronal membrane.
At rest, mechanosensitive channels including Piezo, TREK/TRAAK, and TRP family members sit closed alongside NMDA receptors.

These channels open in response to sonication-induced membrane deformation from mechanical vibration: Piezo and TRP channels are non-selective and conduct calcium and sodium inward, while opening TREK and TRAAK channels conducts potassium outward.
NMDA receptors are also responsive to mechanical force.
The calcium influx recruits additional voltage-and calcium-gated channels and engages calcium-dependent signaling.
Downstream, this signaling drives expression of immediate early genes and neurotrophic factors, providing a route by which a sonication lasting seconds can produce long-lasting synaptic changes.
Additional proposed mechanisms, including flexoelectric e0ects, sonoporation, microtubule resonance, lipid rafts, and a possible thermal contribution, are not visually highlighted here.
